t.taj mahal@27.2,78.0:
Everyone knows the picture, and the odd thing is that the real thing still lives up to it. The Taj Mahal stands on the south bank of the Yamuna in Agra, a city of about one and a half million people, and was commissioned by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. Building took about two decades, with some twenty thousand workers and craftsmen, and the white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, hundreds of kilometres away. Inlay work of semi-precious stones decorates the tomb, and the calligraphy around the great arches is cleverly sized so that the letters seem equal in height from the ground.

What makes it more than a pretty building is its geometry. The tomb sits at the end of a long garden divided by water channels into four parts, and the four minarets lean very slightly outward, so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb. The marble changes colour with the hour, pale pink at dawn, white at noon and golden at sunset. A legend says Shah Jahan planned a black twin across the river, but there is no evidence of it. He was later imprisoned by his son Aurangzeb in the Agra Fort, from where he could see the tomb through a window.

Riding to the Taj is a lesson in Indian traffic. Agra is dense, with auto-rickshaws, cycle-rickshaws, buses, cows and pedestrians crowding the roads, and the horn is part of the language. Vehicles powered by fuel are kept away from the monument itself to protect the marble, so you park at a designated area and walk or take an electric shuttle. The Yamuna Expressway from Delhi is a fast, well-surfaced road, about three hours at moderate speed, and an excellent ride early in the morning before the trucks. In winter, fog can reduce visibility to a few metres, so check conditions.

The monument is closed on Fridays, when it is used for prayer at the mosque beside it, and tickets for foreign visitors cost far more than for Indians, which is worth knowing. Go at sunrise to avoid the worst of the heat and the crowds. Fuel is plentiful in Agra, and the city has plenty of hotels with secure parking. Try petha, a translucent sweet made from ash gourd, and a plate of parathas in the old bazaar. Be patient with touts and keep valuables close, but do not let that spoil the moment you walk through the gateway and see the dome for the first time.
t.kochi@9.9,76.3:
Kochi is the old spice port of Kerala, and it still has the look of a place where traders from many countries have come and gone. Arab, Chinese, Portuguese, Dutch and British merchants all passed through, and the old quarter around Fort Kochi keeps traces of them: Chinese fishing nets on the waterfront, a Portuguese-era church, a synagogue in Jew Town and colonial houses facing the water. The city itself is spread across islands and the mainland, tied together by bridges and ferries, with a lot of water around.

Kochi is a very practical place to start. It is a big, busy city, so fuel stations, cafes, hotels and mechanics are everywhere, and you can find almost anything you need before heading inland. The hard part is traffic. City roads are crowded with buses, auto-rickshaws, scooters and trucks, and the drivers are quick and inventive, so the first hour is more about patience than pleasure. Leave early in the morning, before the heat and the congestion build, and you will be out of the built-up area faster.

The ride east toward Munnar is the reward. As the land rises from the coastal plain into the Western Ghats, the roads wind through rubber plantations, spice gardens and patches of forest, and the air gets cooler. Tea terraces cover the hills around Munnar in a deep green patchwork. This part of India is one of the wettest, with the south-west monsoon arriving around June, so the drier months from roughly October to March are the more comfortable ones for riding.

Food is worth some attention. Kerala cooking uses coconut, curry leaves, mustard seed and black pepper in ways that are quite different from the north, and fish curry with rice, appam with stew and a simple banana-leaf meal are all good ways to eat here. Fresh seafood is plentiful near the waterfront.

Treat Kochi as a starting line and a homecoming. It is an energetic, humid port city, and after a day in the hills, the ceiling fan and the cold drink at the end are a welcome sight.
t.diamantina@-18.2,-43.6:
Diamantina earned its name the hard way. In the early 1720s, prospectors in the hills of Minas Gerais found diamonds in the gravel of the streams, and for the next hundred years this high, rocky corner of Brazil supplied most of the world's stones. The Portuguese Crown clamped down at once, declaring a restricted diamond district, with a monopoly on trade, permits, soldiers and informers, and the town that grew up at the centre of it, on a cold plateau in the Serra do Espinhaço at around 1,200 metres, became rich and strange. Today it has about thirty-seven thousand people, and the colonial centre was inscribed by UNESCO in 1999.

The best-known resident was a woman, Chica da Silva, born into slavery, who became the companion of the wealthy contractor who held the diamond rights, and who ran a household with an authority that scandalised and fascinated her contemporaries. Her story has been told in books, films and a famous television series. More than a century later, the town produced another famous figure: Juscelino Kubitschek, born here in 1902, who became president of Brazil and built Brasília. His modest childhood house is a museum.

The old town is built of whitewashed walls, wooden balconies, carved doors and ochre-tiled roofs, laid out on steep, cobbled streets that climb in all directions. The cobbles are rough river stones, slippery in the rain and unkind to a bike, and several streets in the historic centre are narrow and steep enough that you will want to park and walk. The famous Vesperata, when musicians play from the balconies on certain evenings in the dry season, fills the streets with brass and crowds, and it is worth planning around if the date fits.

The roads that lead here follow the old Estrada Real, the Royal Road, along which gold and diamonds went to the coast and goods came back. They climb through bare, stony uplands of quartzite, grass and rock, with great skies and long views, and the curves are generous. Surfaces vary widely, from fresh asphalt to potholed stretches, and cattle sometimes drift onto the road. Fog can fill the plateau in the morning, and in the rainy months from November to March, afternoon storms are heavy.

Diamantina has fuel stations and all the services of a small city, and it is the best place to fill up before the long stretches south. Eat feijão tropeiro, a dish of beans, farofa, sausage and egg that was once the muleteers' food, and try the strong local cheese. The dry months, from May to September, are the best, though nights are cold at this altitude, so take a warm layer.
t.fatehpur sikri@27.1,77.7:
Fatehpur Sikri rises on a sandstone ridge west of Agra, a red city of palaces, courtyards and mosques built by the Mughal emperor Akbar in the 1570s and abandoned just a few years later. Akbar built it to honour the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, who had predicted the birth of his son and heir, and for over a decade it was the capital of his empire. Then, for reasons that are still debated, perhaps a lack of water or political changes, the court moved away, and the city was left almost intact, a time capsule of Mughal architecture and a World Heritage site.

The palace complex is a series of courtyards and pavilions, including the Diwan-i-Khas, with its extraordinary central pillar supporting a circular platform where Akbar is said to have sat during discussions with scholars of different religions. The Panch Mahal, a five-storey pavilion with open columns, caught the breezes in the hot summer. Next door, the Jama Masjid, one of the largest mosques in India, is entered through the Buland Darwaza, a towering gate built to celebrate Akbar's victories in Gujarat. Inside the mosque courtyard, the white marble tomb of Salim Chishti is a place of pilgrimage, where visitors tie threads to the screens and make wishes.

The riding in this region is hot, dusty and chaotic. The road from Agra to Fatehpur Sikri is busy with trucks, buses, tractors, cows and pedestrians, and Indian traffic follows its own logic, with the biggest vehicle generally having the right of way. Surfaces vary from good to terrible, and speed breakers appear without warning. Ride defensively and expect the unexpected. The best time to visit is from October to March, when the temperatures are bearable; summer is scorching, and the monsoon brings heavy rain.

Not far away, the Keoladeo National Park at Bharatpur, another World Heritage site, is one of the finest bird sanctuaries in Asia, with herons, storks, cranes and many migratory birds in winter. You can explore it by bicycle or rickshaw. And of course, Agra, with the Taj Mahal and the Agra Fort, is just forty kilometres east.

Fatehpur Sikri town, below the ridge, has fuel, food stalls and basic accommodation. Agra has everything you need. Beware of touts and unofficial guides at the site; hire an official guide if you want one. Try a plate of petha, the translucent sweet made from ash gourd, a speciality of Agra.
t.agra fort@27.2,78.0:
Red sandstone walls rise out of the Yamuna floodplain at Agra, and for a moment they seem to have been put there to distract you from the Taj Mahal. Agra Fort is a very different thing from its famous neighbour, two and a half kilometres downstream. It is a palace-city, a military stronghold and a seat of government, begun by the emperor Akbar in 1565 and completed over several generations, with high double walls, a moat and gates that climb in zigzags to slow down attackers. UNESCO listed it in 1983.

Inside, the buildings change character as you walk. Akbar's red sandstone halls, carved with the confidence of a young empire, give way to the white marble of his grandson Shah Jahan, the builder of the Taj, who added the Pearl Mosque, the Hall of Public Audience and the Hall of Private Audience. Shah Jahan ended his life here, imprisoned in a marble pavilion by his son Aurangzeb, and he is said to have spent his last years looking across the river at the tomb he built for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Whether or not the story is exact, the view from the pavilion, through a haze of dust and woodsmoke, is the right place to understand it.

Riding to Agra from Delhi is not a gentle introduction to India. The fastest route, the Yamuna Expressway, is generally closed to two-wheelers, so riders use the older national highway through Mathura, which is crowded with trucks, buses, tractors, cows and other things that do not follow lanes. Keep left, expect the horn to be a means of communication, and avoid riding after dark. Winter, from November to February, has the best weather but can bring thick morning fog, and the summer heat is extreme, often above forty degrees.

Agra has a big appetite for sweets, and petha, a translucent candy made from ash gourd, is sold everywhere. Mughlai food, with rich curries and kebabs, is the local style, and the leather and marble crafts are the traditional trades.

Agra has well over a million people, so fuel, food and accommodation are everywhere. Arrive at the fort early, since the day heats up quickly, and carry water.
t.keoladeo national park@27.2,77.5:
For decades the Maharajas of Bharatpur kept this marshland as a duck-shooting estate, and the scale of the sport is hard to believe. On a single day in 1938 the viceroy Lord Linlithgow and his party shot more than four thousand birds, a record that still shocks people today. The shoots ended after independence, and in 1971 the area became a protected sanctuary. It is now Keoladeo National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1985 and one of the finest bird sanctuaries in Asia.

The landscape is a patchwork of wetlands, grassland and scrubby woodland, laid out by the Maharajas with low embankments that hold water during the monsoon. In winter it becomes a crowded haven for hundreds of species. Painted storks and spoonbills nest in the trees, cranes stalk the shallows, and migratory ducks arrive from Central Asia and Siberia. The Siberian crane, once the park's most celebrated winter visitor, no longer comes, which is a sad story, but the sarus crane, the tallest flying bird in the world, still lives here and can be seen dancing in the fields. Look in the trees for owls and in the grass for pythons basking in the sun.

Motor vehicles are not allowed inside, so you leave the bike at the gate and move on foot, by bicycle or in a cycle rickshaw whose driver doubles as a surprisingly good bird guide. The paths are flat and shady, and the best time for birds is early morning in winter, when the mist rises off the water and the light is golden. Bring binoculars if you have them, and a hat. Mosquitoes can be fierce near the water.

In the nearby town of Bharatpur, the Lohagarh Fort, the Iron Fort, held out against several British sieges in the early nineteenth century. The town is a plain, busy place, but it has good sweets and tea.

The ride from Agra, about fifty kilometres west, is a mix of highway and rural roads, with crowds, trucks and cattle. Fuel is available in Bharatpur, a city of over two hundred thousand, a few kilometres from the park. Avoid the monsoon and the hot season, April to September, when the park is quiet.
t.delhi@28.6,77.2:
Delhi is a city of layers, and every dynasty that wanted to rule northern India seems to have built its own version here. The Qutub Minar, a 73-metre tower of red sandstone, was begun in the late twelfth century; the great Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid in the seventeenth century; and in the twentieth century the British laid out New Delhi with its wide avenues, India Gate and the long processional road up to the Presidential Palace. Old Delhi, around Chandni Chowk, is a maze of lanes, spice markets and food stalls where paratha shops have been frying bread in ghee for generations.

It is huge and loud and a challenge, but a rewarding one if you take it slowly. The food is the best reason to stay: kebabs and biryani in the lanes near the mosque, chaat and lassi on every corner, and tandoori dishes and butter chicken in the restaurants. The Lodhi Gardens and Humayun's Tomb, built in the sixteenth century and a precursor of the Taj Mahal, are calm places to rest in the heat. The Yamuna river runs through the east side of the city, though it is far from clean.

For a rider, Delhi is mostly a place to start and finish. Traffic is dense and chaotic, with lanes ignored, horns constant, and buses, rickshaws and cows in the mix, so ride defensively and expect any vehicle to do anything. The Ring Road and the expressways are quicker, but avoid the rush hours, and leave before dawn if you can. Heading north to Rishikesh and the Himalaya or south-west toward Jaipur, you get onto good highways within an hour, and the real riding begins. Air pollution is severe from October to January, and visibility can be low, so a mask and a clear visor help. In May and June the heat can reach 45 degrees.

Fuel stations are everywhere, in a city of many millions, and food is available at all hours. Pick a hotel with secure parking, because bikes are targeted by thieves in some areas, and check the rules about older vehicles and permits if you bring a bike from outside the city. Take a day to see the Red Fort and the old city by rickshaw before you leave, and arrive at the start of the ride rested.
t.tirunelveli@9.5,77.2:
It sits on the Thamirabarani river in the far south of Tamil Nadu, with its twin town of Palayamkottai across the water, a former garrison that earned the nickname Oxford of the South for its colleges and schools. The big Nellaiappar temple, with its musical stone pillars, anchors the old town, and the city's other claim to fame is halwa, a dense, glossy sweet of wheat, ghee and sugar that people carry home in boxes. The river water is said to be the secret.

At roughly 9.5 degrees north and 77.2 east, it falls in the Western Ghats on the Tamil Nadu side of the border with Kerala, in the green fold of mountains near Gudalur and Cumbum, a good twenty kilometres from the nearest sizeable town. The Cardamom Hills rise here to the west, and the vegetation changes quickly with altitude from dry scrub and tamarind on the Tamil plains to wet evergreen forest, cardamom shade and tea on the cooler heights. Rubber and spice estates fill much of the lower ground.

Riding through this belt is a pleasure of hairpins and shade. The ghat road between Cumbum and Kumily climbs in a long series of bends through banana and grape farms, then enters forest on the Kerala side, where macaques sit on the crash barriers and the air smells of damp earth and cardamom. Surfaces vary, with smooth sections and sudden potholes after the monsoon, and trucks carrying produce and pilgrims make blind corners something to treat with respect. Early morning, before the trucks wake up, is the best time, with mist in the valleys and a low sun on the hills.

Once you climb into the hills, assume services thin out, so start with a full tank. Street food in the towns is cheap and very good; a plate of parotta with salna, a spiced gravy, is the sensible lunch, and filter coffee in a steel tumbler is the sensible finish. The monsoons, from June to September and again in October and November, bring heavy rain, so plan for dry months.
t.periyar tiger reserve@9.5,77.2:
Periyar is one of the best-known wildlife reserves in India, and it owes its lake to a dam. In 1895 the British, working for the Madras Presidency, completed the Mullaperiyar Dam across the Periyar river and sent water east through a tunnel into the dry plains of Tamil Nadu, flooding a forested valley in the process. What drowned the old trees created the main attraction: a long, winding lake with skeletons of old trunks poking through the surface, and around it a reserve of evergreen and deciduous forest, home to wild elephants, gaur, sambar, wild boar, lion-tailed macaques and a small number of tigers. The dam is still a point of dispute between Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

The Kerala side is wetter, and the contrast is quick: within thirty kilometres the plains give way to moist forest, spice plantations and the little tourist town of Kumily, whose bazaar sells cardamom, pepper, cinnamon and tea. Thekkady, the park gate, is a few minutes beyond. Inside the reserve is the Sabarimala hill shrine, reached by pilgrims in their millions in the winter season.

Getting here from the plains is a ride in itself. The ghat road climbs from Cumbum in dozens of bends, past vineyards and tomato fields, and crosses the state line into forest, with fine views back over the plains. The surface is mostly tarmac, rough in places, and in the pilgrim season, from November to January, the road is crowded with buses and cars. Elephants sometimes cross the road at dusk, and monkeys are a nuisance, so keep your snacks sealed and your speed down.

Boat safaris on the lake run through the day, though the most rewarding time is early morning, when animals come to drink and mist hangs on the water. Entry rules change, so book ahead. Fuel is at Kumily and Cumbum, the latter a town of sixty thousand about thirty kilometres away. Kumily's cafés serve good appam with stew, and spice shops sell fresh cardamom by the bag, which smells wonderful in a pannier.
t.ranni forest division@9.5,77.2:
Ranni's forests are the kind of mixed evergreen and moist deciduous woodland that once covered much of Kerala, with teak and rosewood, wild jackfruit and rubber plantations in the lower reaches. The Pamba flows down from the hills through Ranni town toward the backwaters, and every winter its banks are crowded with pilgrims heading up to the Sabarimala shrine, a journey of faith that has shaped the road network here. The town itself is a small market place, with a bus stand, a bridge over the river and rows of shops selling bananas, spices and rubber sheets.

For a rider, this side of Kerala is soft and green rather than dramatic. Roads run through coconut palms and rubber trees in long, easy curves, over small bridges and past roadside shrines, and with traffic mild in the mornings it is relaxing. The climb toward the hills is gradual, giving shaded views over valley paddies, and in the monsoon the roads are slick with leaves and rain. Buses are the main hazard, taking the middle of the road, and the pilgrim season from November to January brings a long procession of vehicles.

Ranni itself, to the west in Kerala, is well supplied with petrol pumps and small restaurants serving fish curry and rice or fried banana. Forest areas may need permits to enter, and the Forest Department can tell you which tracks are open. Bring rain gear, because showers arrive quickly, and carry your documents as police checks are routine.
t.srivilliputtur wildlife sanctuary@9.5,77:
Srivilliputtur sits at the foot of the Western Ghats in the dry south of Tamil Nadu, and its great gift to the world is a tower. The temple of Andal, a female saint of the Vaishnava tradition, has a gopuram of eleven tiers that rises above the town and is used as the emblem of the Tamil Nadu government. Inside, the rituals continue much as they have for centuries, and the town's other famous product is palkova, a sweet milk fudge, said to be better here than anywhere else. A bite of it and a glass of strong tea is a good break on a hot day.

The wildlife sanctuary the label names covers the hills above the town and has now been combined with the neighbouring Megamalai sanctuary into a tiger reserve. It is the home of the grizzled giant squirrel, a large, shy animal with a long bushy tail that lives in the tops of the trees, and the area also holds elephants, gaur, sambar and a rich collection of birds. The terrain climbs from dry deciduous forest to moist evergreen and then to high grassland, and the streams that run off it feed the plains.

The ghat roads here climb steeply in bends that reward careful riding, with sudden views of the Tamil plain and distant haze, and on a clear morning the farms and temples of the plain look like a map. Landslides in the monsoon can close sections, and the roads are narrow and shared with bullock carts, buses, goats and tractors, so ride within yourself. Gravel and potholes are common after the rains.

Services are scarce in the hills, so fill up in Cumbum or Gudalur, the nearest larger towns, before you climb. Gudalur has a bazaar and food stalls, and a plate of idli with coconut chutney is enough to set you up for a morning. Entry to the sanctuary needs permission from the Forest Department, so ask in advance if you plan to leave the road. The best months are from October to February, when the days are cool and dry.
t.achankovil forest division@9.5,77.2:
The Achankovil Forest Division is named for a river, and the river is named for a temple. The Achankovil flows west from the high ridges of the Western Ghats in southern Kerala through Pathanamthitta and Alappuzha districts, and on its banks stands the ancient Achankovil shrine to Sastha, a deity honoured by pilgrims on their way to Sabarimala. The valley it cuts is one of the main passes between Kerala and Tamil Nadu, the Achankovil gap, which allowed traders, armies and spices to cross the range for centuries.

So when you are standing here, the Achankovil forests are on the other side of the ridge, to the west and south-west, in a very different, wetter world. There the woodland is tall evergreen and moist deciduous, with strangler figs, tree ferns and enormous bamboo clumps, and the fauna includes elephants, Nilgiri langur and the Malabar giant squirrel. In the monsoon every stream is a torrent.

The riding here is a story of two slopes. On the Tamil side the roads are drier and straighter, with hairpins crossing the face of the escarpment, and the vegetation turns suddenly from thorn scrub to forest at the crest. On the Kerala side the roads wind between plantations of rubber, pepper and cardamom, and every bend has a tea stall or temple. Surfaces are better than you might expect, and traffic is calm outside the pilgrim season, though buses and trucks require respect on the narrow bends.

Services are in the towns. Gudalur and Cumbum on the Tamil side have fuel and food, and on the Kerala side Kumily and Pathanamthitta are the places to look for pumps. A hot cup of tea from a roadside stall is a ritual here, often with a banana fritter, and the forest rest houses can sometimes be booked through the Forest Department. If you plan to enter the forest tracks, check access first, and carry rain gear at all times, because storms arrive suddenly.
t.konni forest division@9.5,77.2:
Konni has a place in Kerala's affections for one reason above all: elephants. The Konni elephant camp, on the banks of the Achankovil river, is among the oldest in the state, and for generations it was where wild elephants, caught and tamed, were trained to work in the forests and temples. Today the practice is over, but the camp still looks after elephants and their calves, and children come to watch them being bathed in the river in the morning. It is a gentle, rather moving place, with an unhurried atmosphere.

The forest division around it covers a large area of Pathanamthitta district, a landscape of rolling hills with teak plantations, rubber estates and patches of moist evergreen forest. Konni's teak was planted in the nineteenth century and is among the oldest plantations in Kerala. So you are on the dry side of the range, looking back at the long wall of ridges where the clouds pile up on the Kerala slopes.

The ride across the divide, if you do it, is a lesson in contrasts. On the Tamil side the road climbs from hot, flat farmland through grapevines and coconut groves into cooler hills, and over the top you meet forest, damp air and the smell of cardamom. Down the western side the road is shaded, with long curves, tea shops and places where elephants have worn paths across the tarmac, which is why signs warn you to slow down. In the evening, they are best avoided.

The practical needs are simple. Take on petrol in Gudalur or Cumbum before you cross, and again in Kumily on the Kerala side. Konni town on the western side has pumps and small restaurants serving the usual Kerala breakfast of puttu and kadala curry, which is cheap and filling. If you want to visit the camp, ask locally about opening times, as these change, and remember to be quiet and keep a respectful distance from the animals. The roads can be slippery in the rains from June to September, so be careful.
t.belo horizonte@-19.9,-43.9:
Belo Horizonte means beautiful horizon, and the name comes from the ridge of the Serra do Curral that closes the view to the south of town. It is a large city, a bit over two million people, and unusually for Brazil it was planned: it was laid out in the 1890s as the new capital of Minas Gerais, replacing Ouro Preto, with wide avenues and a grid cut across by diagonal boulevards. The result is a place that feels more ordered than many Brazilian cities, though traffic is dense and the hills make it a rider's workout.

Mineiros are proud of their food, and BH is the capital of that pride. Pão de queijo, the little cheese bread, appears at every café counter, and the Mercado Central is a maze of stalls selling cheeses, cachaça, sausages and sweets. Bars are famous for botecos, informal spots with cold beer and snacks, and the city has been called the bar capital of Brazil. Try feijão tropeiro, a dish of beans, sausage and manioc flour, and the tutu, a bean purée, if you have a big appetite.

The architecture is a surprise. The Pampulha complex, designed in the early 1940s by Oscar Niemeyer, with its curving church of São Francisco de Assis covered in blue-and-white tiles, is on UNESCO's list, and the lake beside it makes a nice place for an evening walk. In the old days, gold and iron attracted people to the region, and the mountains south of the city still hold many mines, which explains the name of the state, General Mines.

For riders, Belo Horizonte is the gateway to the Estrada Real, the old Royal Road, and to the colonial towns of Ouro Preto and Mariana, about a hundred kilometres to the south-east, where the best riding begins. Leave early to avoid the heavy traffic on the ring road and the main highways, and expect trucks. Fuel, repairs and parts for most brands are easy to find here, with Nova Lima and Contagem making up the rest of the metropolitan area. Weather is warm and pleasant, with a wet summer.
t.serra do cipo@-19.3,-43.6:
At the southern end of the Espinhaço range, the long backbone of rock that runs through Minas Gerais and Bahia, the Serra do Cipó is a country of bare quartzite ridges, clear streams and waterfalls that glow amber from the tannins in the water. The national park protects a landscape of campos rupestres, rocky fields where wildflowers and strange plants have adapted to thin, acid soil, and where you find species that exist nowhere else on Earth. Among them are the canelas-de-ema, tall, shaggy-trunked plants that look like something from a children's book.

The highway MG-010 runs through the range and is the reason to be here on a bike. Heading north from the Belo Horizonte area toward Conceição do Mato Dentro, and on toward Diamantina, it climbs and dips over ridges in long, open bends, with views of rock outcrops and grasslands stretching to the horizon. Traffic is moderate, though lorries and tourist vehicles slow things on weekends, and the weather can bring sudden fog and heavy summer storms, so stay alert. The surface is mostly paved but varies, and it is worth watching for loose gravel near the edges.

The route belongs to the old Estrada Real, along which gold and later diamonds were carried to the coast in colonial times, and Diamantina, at the north end, is a colonial town built on the diamond trade, with a historic centre listed by UNESCO. The cultural ties are strong here: fine silverwork, folk music and the Vesperata, a tradition of musicians playing from balconies in the evening, are all part of the region's character.

Cachoeira Véu da Noiva and Cachoeira da Farofa, among others, are reached on short paths, and clear pools invite a quick swim after a hot ride. Conceição do Mato Dentro, about thirty-eight kilometres away with over ten thousand people, is the nearest town of size, and the best bet for fuel, so fill up before the park. Carry water and sun protection, because the open ridges have little shade, and keep a layer for cool evenings at altitude.
t.taldykorgan@45.0,78.4:
Taldykorgan is the capital of the Zhetysu region, a calm, green city on the plain at the foot of the Dzungarian Alatau. Zhetysu means seven rivers, a name that comes from the streams running down from the mountains into the basin around Lake Balkhash, and it has long been a corridor for nomads and traders. The city has around a hundred and sixteen thousand people and an easy, orderly feel, with wide avenues, parks and clean public spaces. Behind it, the snow-capped range gleams on clear days, and the nearby foothills are a popular weekend escape.

It is not a city of famous monuments. For history you look to the surrounding region, which is dotted with ancient burial mounds, petroglyphs and the traces of old Silk Road routes, and to the Dzungarian people who once ruled this land and whose name the mountains carry. Local museums outline the region's story, and nearby are tracts of orchards and farms that produce apples and other fruit. The region itself was reorganised in recent years, and Taldykorgan took on the role of capital of the newly formed administrative unit.

Riding here is a matter of long, easy highways across open steppe. The road between Almaty and Taldykorgan is generally good, busy with trucks, and punctuated by speed limits near villages. Spring brings green grass and flowers, summer is hot and dry, and autumn is crisp and golden, with early snow possible on the mountains. Wind is frequent, and sudden storms can sweep across the plain. If you head east toward Altyn Emel or south toward the Ili river, the roads become quieter and more open.

For the traveller, Taldykorgan is a convenient and comfortable stop. There is fuel, there are supermarkets, hotels and cafes, and the food is typical Kazakh fare: beshbarmak, plov, samsa and plenty of tea. It is a good place to eat, rest and plan the next section, and it suits riders who want to break a long day without sacrificing comfort. Fill up the tank and check your supplies before you leave, since the stretches beyond town are wide and sparsely served.
